docs.title: About Me
docs.text:
I am a PhD research scholar at the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay (2024–ongoing), working at the intersection of material science, plant biology, and soil microbiology. My research focuses on synthesizing biochar from aquatic weeds via slow pyrolysis and investigating its role as a soil amendment for promoting crop growth. I trace phenotypic effects down to the genotypic level and study community-level shifts in native soil microbiota under prolonged biochar exposure. I am also employing DFT-based computational methods to simulate electronic communication at the biochar–microbe interface — a novel frontier in understanding Extracellular Electron Transfer (EET) in soil systems.

I hold a B.Sc. in Botany Honours from Shri Shikshayatan College (University of Calcutta) and an M.Sc. from Presidency University, West Bengal (CGPA: 8.9/10). With nine peer-reviewed publications spanning plant physiology, mycology, bioinformatics, and ecology, I am committed to science that bridges molecular mechanisms and real-world environmental challenges.

docs.title: Functional Characterization of Effectors in Magnaporthe oryzae
docs.text: Type Research Internship (with fellowship) Funding SERB-DST, Government of India Supervisor Dr. Nazmiara Sabnam, Assistant Professor, Presidency University, Kolkata Pathogen Magnaporthe oryzae (rice-blast pathogen) Output Peer-reviewed publication in Journal of Biomolecular Structure and Dynamics (2023)

docs.title: Background
docs.text: Magnaporthe oryzae is the causal agent of rice blast, one of the most devastating fungal diseases of rice globally. A key virulence mechanism of this pathogen is the secretion of effector proteins into host cells — small molecules that manipulate host immunity and facilitate infection. Understanding these effectors at the structural and biophysical level is essential for developing durable resistance strategies.

docs.title: Study A — Secretome-Wide Intrinsic Disorder Analysis
docs.text:
Scale: ~365 small secretory effector molecules from the complete M. oryzae secretome

Bioinformatic pipeline:

  1. Identified putative effectors using criteria: presence of a signal peptide, absence of transmembrane domains, and confirmed signal peptide cleavage site
  2. Used FoldIndex to quantify intrinsic disorder, infoldability, charge, and hydrophobicity for all 365 effectors
  3. Classified effectors into six structural categories:
Class Description Ordered Predominantly structured proteins Mostly ordered Slight tendency toward flexibility Moderately disordered Mixed structure–disorder Mostly disordered Largely unstructured Highly disordered Minimal structured regions Extremely disordered Almost entirely unstructured

Significance: Intrinsic disorder in effectors is functionally important — disordered regions enable binding to multiple host targets, facilitate translocation, and confer adaptability to host immune pressure.

docs.title: Study B — Molecular-Level Characterization of Three Hypothetical Effectors
docs.text:
Three hypothetical effector genes were selected for in-depth analysis:

  • Natural intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)
  • Percentage disorder across the full sequence
  • Phosphorylation sites in the amino acid sequence
  • Possible protein domains and their predicted functions
  • Post-translational modification (PTM) sites

docs.title: MS Dissertation — Stress-Responsive Gene Promoters in Brassicaceae
docs.text: Institution Presidency University, West Bengal Laboratory Plant Molecular Biology Supervisor Dr. Malay Das, Assistant Professor Degree M.Sc. Botany (2021) Approach Bioinformatic / Computational

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This dissertation investigated how plants at different ends of the stress-tolerance spectrum regulate their stress-responsive genes at the promoter level. By comparing two species — the highly stress-tolerant Thellungiella salsuginea and the stress-sensitive model plant Arabidopsis thaliana — the project aimed to identify promoter-level regulatory differences that may explain their contrasting abilities to cope with osmotic stress.

docs.title: Gene Families Studied
docs.text:
Four gene families with known stress-responsive roles in Brassicaceae were selected:

Gene Family Role DREB1 Dehydration-Responsive Element Binding factors — cold and drought response SWEET Sugar Will Eventually be Exported Transporters — osmotic and biotic stress LIM LIM-domain proteins — cytoskeletal remodelling under stress ANNEXIN Calcium-dependent membrane-binding proteins — abiotic stress signalling

docs.title: Study Species
docs.text:
• Thellungiella salsuginea (salt cress) — extreme halophyte and drought-tolerant species; a natural model for stress tolerance in Brassicaceae
  • Arabidopsis thaliana — well-characterized stress-sensitive model plant

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
• Retrieval of promoter sequences (upstream regulatory regions) from public genome databases
  • Identification and comparative analysis of cis-regulatory elements within promoters
  • Statistical analysis of element frequency differences between the two species
  • Functional annotation of discovered motifs using plant transcription factor databases

docs.title: Key Questions Addressed
docs.text:
1. Do stress-tolerant T. salsuginea and stress-sensitive A. thaliana differ in the types or density of cis-regulatory elements in the promoters of these four gene families?
  2. Which regulatory motifs may confer superior stress responsiveness in T. salsuginea?
  3. Can promoter architecture alone explain part of the phenotypic difference in osmotic stress tolerance between the two species?

docs.title: PhD Research — Biochar, Crop Growth & Soil Microbiology
docs.text: Institution Indian Institute of Technology Bombay Duration 2024 – ongoing Current GPI 8.83 Focus areas Material synthesis · Plant biology · Soil microbiology · Computational chemistry

docs.title: Research Overview
docs.text: This PhD project sits at the convergence of material science, plant biology, and environmental microbiology. The central material is biochar — a carbon-rich product formed by the thermal degradation (slow pyrolysis) of organic feedstocks such as aquatic weeds or agricultural waste — and the overarching question is how its incorporation into soil reshapes plant growth and the microbial community that lives within it.

docs.title: 1. Biochar Synthesis
docs.text:
Synthesizing biochar via slow pyrolysis from:

  • Aquatic weeds (locally abundant, problematic biomass)
  • Agricultural waste residues

Characterizing the resulting material for surface properties, carbon content, and functional groups relevant to soil–plant–microbe interactions.

docs.title: 2. Soil Amendment & Crop Growth
docs.text:
Applying biochar as a soil amendment and tracking its effects on crop growth at two levels:

  • Phenotypic: plant height, biomass, root morphology, yield
  • Genotypic: expression of developmental genes involved in growth promotion — tracing phenotypic outcomes to their molecular basis

Current result: Biochar derived from aquatic weeds shows a statistically significant positive impact on mustard (Brassica juncea) plant growth. This work is being prepared for publication.

docs.title: 3. Soil Microbial Community Dynamics
docs.text:
Studying how prolonged biochar exposure in the soil shifts the native microbial community:

  • Community profiling at genus and species level
  • Identifying taxa that increase or decrease in abundance under biochar treatment
  • Hypothesis: biochar acts as a selective habitat, favouring electroactive and carbon-utilizing microorganisms

docs.title: 4. Extracellular Electron Transfer (EET) — Quantum-Level Interactions
docs.text:
The most novel component of this work: modelling the electronic communication between biochar surfaces and soil microbes using DFT (Density Functional Theory) simulations.

  • Simulating electronic signatures at the carbon surface–cell wall/protein interface
  • Understanding the quantum-level basis of EET between biochar and microbes
  • This layer of analysis links material chemistry directly to microbial physiology
